subject: biology

moments.title: Hooke sees 'cells'
moments.body: Hooke's 'Micrographia' shows the honeycomb structure of cork seen through his microscope. He calls them 'cells' after monastic rooms.
moments.takeaway: The word 'cell' is born — applied to dead plant walls.

moments.title: Schleiden and Schwann
moments.body: Schleiden states all plants are made of cells; Schwann extends it to animals. Cells become the universal unit of life.

moments.title: Virchow's 'omnis cellula e cellula'
moments.body: Virchow declares every cell comes from a pre-existing cell. Spontaneous generation is finally rejected for cellular life.
moments.takeaway: Cells reproduce. The cell theory is complete.

moments.title: Single-cell biology
moments.body: Single-cell RNA-sequencing identifies thousands of distinct cell types in the human body. The Human Cell Atlas project aims to catalogue them all.
moments.takeaway: Cell theory now operates at single-cell resolution.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Single-cell omics and live-cell imaging now reveal cellular diversity in unprecedented detail. The Human Cell Atlas is mapping all human cell types.
now.open_questions: How many distinct cell types exist in the human body?

reflection: Hooke saw dead walls and named them 'cells'. The name stuck though it was misleading. How does early terminology shape later science?
